claim: The fish-hunting marine cone snail Conus geographus uses a specialized venom insulin to induce hypoglycemic shock in its prey.
source: The fish-hunting marine cone snail Conus geographus uses a specialized venom insulin to induce hypoglycemic shock in its prey.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Safavi-Hemami et al., 2015; Robinson and Safavi-Hemami, 2016) as referenced in the Introduction section.

claim: Con-Ins G1 has unique characteristics relevant to the design of new insulin therapeutics.
source: We recently showed that this venom insulin, Con-Ins G1, has unique characteristics relevant to the design of new insulin therapeutics.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work as indicated in the Abstract.

claim: Insulins from C. geographus, Conus tulipa and Conus kinoshitai exhibit diverse sequences.
source: Insulins from C. geographus, Conus tulipa and Conus kinoshitai exhibit diverse sequences, yet all bind to and activate the human insulin receptor.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence data presented in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: All insulins from C. geographus, Conus tulipa and Conus kinoshitai bind to and activate the human insulin receptor.
source: Insulins from C. geographus, Conus tulipa and Conus kinoshitai exhibit diverse sequences, yet all bind to and activate the human insulin receptor.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Venom insulins significantly lower blood glucose in the streptozotocin-induced model of diabetes in zebrafish.
source: When tested in zebrafish and mice, venom insulins significantly lower blood glucose in the streptozotocin-induced model of diabetes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Venom insulins significantly lower blood glucose in the streptozotocin-induced model of diabetes in mice.
source: When tested in zebrafish and mice, venom insulins significantly lower blood glucose in the streptozotocin-induced model of diabetes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Cone snails have evolved diverse strategies to activate the vertebrate insulin receptor.
source: Our findings suggest that cone snails have evolved diverse strategies to activate the vertebrate insulin receptor and provide unique insight into the design of novel drugs for the treatment of diabetes.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the diverse sequences and activities of venom insulins presented in the manuscript.

claim: Insulin is a pancreatic hormone that is critical for glucose homeostasis.
source: Insulin is a pancreatic hormone that is critical for glucose homeostasis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about insulin function.

claim: Secretion of insulin from pancreatic β-cells triggers the uptake of blood glucose into a variety of tissues, including the liver, skeletal muscle and adipose cells.
source: Secretion of insulin from pancreatic β-cells triggers the uptake of blood glucose into a variety of tissues, including the liver, skeletal muscle and adipose cells.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about insulin function.

claim: Impairment of insulin secretion and/or insensitivity to the insulin produced can lead to the disease diabetes mellitus.
source: Impairment of insulin secretion and/or insensitivity to the insulin produced can lead to the disease diabetes mellitus.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about diabetes.

claim: Three major types of diabetes have been recognized: Type one diabetes (T1D) or autoimmune diabetes, Type two diabetes (T2D) and gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM).
source: To date, three major types of diabetes have been recognized: Type one diabetes (T1D) or autoimmune diabetes, Type two diabetes (T2D) and gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about diabetes classification.

claim: Daily insulin injections are the only effective treatment for patients with T1D, late-stage T2D and some with GDM.
source: Daily insulin injections are the only effective treatment for patients with T1D, late-stage T2D and some with GDM (Mack and Tomich, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mack and Tomich, 2017.

claim: A major limitation of insulin therapy is its delayed action.
source: A major limitation of insulin therapy is its delayed action.
evidence: This is established knowledge about insulin therapy limitations.

claim: The native insulin hormone consists of an A and B chain connected by disulfide bonds.
source: The native hormone (consisting of an A and B chain connected by disulfide bonds) oligomerizes into a stable hexamer comprising three insulin dimers held together by two central zinc ions (Adams et al., 1969).
evidence: This is established knowledge about insulin structure, supported by citation to Adams et al., 1969.

claim: Native insulin oligomerizes into a stable hexamer comprising three insulin dimers held together by two central zinc ions.
source: The native hormone (consisting of an A and B chain connected by disulfide bonds) oligomerizes into a stable hexamer comprising three insulin dimers held together by two central zinc ions (Adams et al., 1969).
evidence: This is established knowledge about insulin structure, supported by citation to Adams et al., 1969.

claim: Following subcutaneous injection, the insulin hexamer has to dissociate into the dimer, then monomer, in order to activate the insulin receptor.
source: Following subcutaneous injection, the hexamer has to dissociate into the dimer, then monomer, in order to activate the insulin receptor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about insulin pharmacokinetics.

claim: Hexamer-to-monomer conversion is a slow process that can lead to a significant delay in glucose control.
source: Hexamer-to-monomer conversion is a slow process that can lead to a significant delay in glucose control.
evidence: This is established knowledge about insulin pharmacokinetics.

claim: The best fast-acting insulin formulations are not truly monomeric and still require 15–90 min to effectively lower blood glucose.
source: However, despite decades of research the best fast-acting insulin formulations are not truly monomeric and still require 15–90 min to effectively lower blood glucose (Elleri et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Elleri et al., 2011.

claim: The C-terminus of the insulin B chain is involved in dimerization of the insulin molecule.
source: this is because the region involved in dimerization of the insulin molecule, the C-terminus of the insulin B chain, is also of critical importance for receptor activation (Menting et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Menting et al., 2013.

claim: The C-terminus of the insulin B chain is of critical importance for receptor activation.
source: this is because the region involved in dimerization of the insulin molecule, the C-terminus of the insulin B chain, is also of critical importance for receptor activation (Menting et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Menting et al., 2013.

claim: Removing the C-terminus of the B chain to generate a fast-acting analog could not be achieved without a near complete loss of biological activity.
source: Until now, removing this region of the B chain in order to generate a fast-acting analog could not be achieved without a near complete loss of biological activity (Bao et al., 1997; De Meyts et al., 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bao et al., 1997 and De Meyts et al., 1978.

claim: Con-Ins G1 was discovered in the venom of the fish-hunting cone snail, Conus geographus.
source: Novel insights for potentially solving this long-standing problem recently came from our discovery of an insulin peptide found in the venom of the fish-hunting cone snail, Conus geographus (Safavi-Hemami et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Safavi-Hemami et al., 2015.

claim: C. geographus belongs to a large genus of predatory marine snails that use their complex venoms for prey capture, defense and competitive interactions.
source: C. geographus belongs to a large genus of predatory marine snails that use their complex venoms for prey capture, defense and competitive interactions (Olivera, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Olivera, 1997.

claim: Con-Ins G1 was shown to rapidly induce insulin shock (dangerously low blood sugar) in its fish prey.
source: C. geographus insulin (Con-Ins G1) was shown to rapidly induce insulin shock (dangerously low blood sugar) in its fish prey (Safavi-Hemami et al., 2015; Robinson and Safavi-Hemami, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Safavi-Hemami et al., 2015 and Robinson and Safavi-Hemami, 2016.

claim: Con-Ins G1 lacks the region of the B chain that is critical for both dimerization and receptor engagement in human insulin.
source: Remarkably, Con-Ins G1 lacks the region of the B chain that is critical for both, dimerization and receptor engagement in human insulin (Safavi-Hemami et al., 2015; Menting et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Safavi-Hemami et al., 2015 and Menting et al., 2016.

claim: Con-Ins G1 is a potent agonist of the human insulin receptor.
source: Despite this, Con-Ins G1 is a potent agonist of the human insulin receptor (Menting et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Menting et al., 2016.

claim: Two residues within the B chain of Con-Ins G1 act as surrogates for the missing C-terminus of the B chain of human insulin.
source: Structure-function studies provided a rationale for this conundrum: two residues within the B chain of Con-Ins G1 act as surrogates for the missing C-terminus of the B chain of human insulin (Menting et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Menting et al., 2016.

claim: Fish-hunting cone snails have evolved a diverse set of B chain minimized insulins as part of their complex predation strategy.
source: Here, we demonstrate that fish-hunting cone snails have evolved a diverse set of B chain minimized insulins as part of their complex predation strategy.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence and functional data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Venom insulins activate the vertebrate insulin receptor in fish, mouse and human.
source: Remarkably, these insulins activate the vertebrate insulin receptor (in fish, mouse and human) but residues previously identified to serve as surrogates for the loss of the B region in Con-Ins G1 are variable.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 2, 3, 4, and 5.

claim: Residues previously identified to serve as surrogates for the loss of the B region in Con-Ins G1 are variable in other venom insulins.
source: Remarkably, these insulins activate the vertebrate insulin receptor (in fish, mouse and human) but residues previously identified to serve as surrogates for the loss of the B region in Con-Ins G1 are variable.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence data in Figure 1B.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations reveal the modus operandi of venom insulins.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations reveal the modus operandi of these unique molecules.
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics data presented in Figure 6 and the Results section.

claim: Reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) combined with whole transcriptome sequencing led to the identification of several distinct insulin sequences in C. geographus and C. tulipa.
source: Reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) combined with whole transcriptome sequencing led to the identification of several distinct insulin sequences in the two cone snail species C. geographus and C. tulipa (Safavi-Hemami et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Safavi-Hemami et al., 2015.

claim: Con-Ins G1 shared highest similarity with fish insulin.
source: Of these sequences, the venom insulin Con-Ins G1 shared highest similarity with fish insulin and was previously selected for functional and structural characterization (Safavi-Hemami et al., 2015; Menting et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Safavi-Hemami et al., 2015 and Menting et al., 2016.

claim: Four additional venom insulins were synthesized and functionally characterized: Con-Ins G3 from C. geographus and Con-Ins T1A, T1B and T2 from C. tulipa.
source: Here, we synthesized and functionally characterized four additional venom insulins from these species with various degrees of sequence divergence: Con-Ins G3 from C. geographus and Con-Ins T1A, T1B and T2 from C. tulipa.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the Results section.

claim: Con-Ins G1 and G3 differ by 32 residues across the entire precursor (22 residues within the A and B chain).
source: Con-Ins G1 and G3 differ by 32 residues across the entire precursor (22 residues within the A and B chain, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and likely represent paralogs originated by gene duplication (Safavi-Hemami et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Con-Ins G1 and G3 likely represent paralogs originated by gene duplication.
source: Con-Ins G1 and G3 differ by 32 residues across the entire precursor (22 residues within the A and B chain, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and likely represent paralogs originated by gene duplication (Safavi-Hemami et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from sequence data and supported by citation to Safavi-Hemami et al., 2016.

claim: Con-Ins T1A and T1B only differ by three residues across their entire precursor sequence.
source: Con-Ins T1A and T1B only differ by three residues across their entire precursor sequence and likely represent allelic variants of the same gene locus.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Con-Ins T1A and T1B likely represent allelic variants of the same gene locus.
source: Con-Ins T1A and T1B only differ by three residues across their entire precursor sequence and likely represent allelic variants of the same gene locus.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from sequence similarity data.

claim: Con-Ins T2 differs at 15 positions across the precursor (13 positions within the A and B chain).
source: Con-Ins T2 differs at 15 positions across the precursor (13 positions within the A and B chain) and likely originates from a distinct gene locus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Con-Ins T2 likely originates from a distinct gene locus.
source: Con-Ins T2 differs at 15 positions across the precursor (13 positions within the A and B chain) and likely originates from a distinct gene locus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from sequence divergence data.

claim: RT-PCR and whole transcriptome sequencing of the venom gland of C. kinoshitai led to the identification of two new insulin sequences, named Con-Ins K1 and Con-Ins K2.
source: In addition to these sequences, we performed RT-PCR and whole transcriptome sequencing of the venom gland of C. kinoshitai leading to the identification of two new insulin sequences, named Con-Ins K1 and Con-Ins K2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental methods described in the manuscript.

claim: The two C. kinoshitai insulin sequences differ at 24 positions, 22 of which fall within the A and B chain.
source: The two C. kinoshitai insulin sequences differ at 24 positions, 22 of which fall within the A and B chain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The C-peptide regions of Con-Ins K1 and Con-Ins K2 are shorter compared to insulins from C. geographus and C. tulipa.
source: Compared to insulins from C. geographus and C. tulipa, the C-peptide regions of Con-Ins K1 and Con-Ins K2 are shorter suggesting an insertion/deletion event of 14 amino acids (14 codons, 42 nucleotides) during the evolution of these peptides.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The shorter C-peptide regions of Con-Ins K1 and Con-Ins K2 suggest an insertion/deletion event of 14 amino acids (14 codons, 42 nucleotides) during the evolution of these peptides.
source: Compared to insulins from C. geographus and C. tulipa, the C-peptide regions of Con-Ins K1 and Con-Ins K2 are shorter suggesting an insertion/deletion event of 14 amino acids (14 codons, 42 nucleotides) during the evolution of these peptides.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from sequence data.

claim: All venom insulins belong to the same gene superfamily of venom gland-specific insulins.
source: As evident by a highly conserved N-terminal signal sequence, all venom insulins belong to the same gene superfamily of venom gland-specific insulins (Safavi-Hemami et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence data and citation to Safavi-Hemami et al., 2016.

claim: Sequence variability is highest within the A and B chain while the signal sequence is conserved.
source: Sequence variability is highest within the A and B chain while the signal sequence is conserved (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The juxtaposition between conserved and hypervariable regions is a common characteristic of cone snail venom toxins.
source: This juxtaposition between conserved and hypervariable regions is a common characteristic of cone snail venom toxins (Woodward et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Woodward et al., 1990.

claim: All seven venom insulins exhibit the cysteine framework of vertebrate insulin (with 4 and 2 cysteines in the A and B chain, respectively).
source: Unlike the endogenous insulins used by cone snails for insulin signaling (Safavi-Hemami et al., 2016), all seven venom insulins exhibit the cysteine framework of vertebrate insulin (with 4 and 2 cysteines in the A and B chain, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: All seven venom insulins lack the C-terminal region of the B chain involved in dimerization and receptor activation of human insulin.
source: Critically, all seven sequences lack the C-terminal region of the B chain involved in dimerization and receptor activation of human insulin (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Insulins from C. geographus and C. tulipa share more sequence similarity to one another than insulins from C. kinoshitai.
source: Insulins from C. geographus and C. tulipa share more sequence similarity to one another than insulins from C. kinoshitai, consistent with the close phylogenetic relationship of these two species (Puillandre et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence data and citation to Puillandre et al., 2014.

claim: Con-Ins K1 and K2 have longer A chain C-termini and B chain N-termini.
source: Con-Ins K1 and K2 have longer A chain C-termini and B chain N-termini and differ in nearly every position from Con-Ins G1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Con-Ins K1 and K2 differ in nearly every position from Con-Ins G1.
source: Con-Ins K1 and K2 have longer A chain C-termini and B chain N-termini and differ in nearly every position from Con-Ins G1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Venom insulins are distinct from the endogenous signaling insulin expressed in the circumoesophageal nerve ring of cone snails.
source: Notably, venom insulins are distinct from the endogenous signaling insulin expressed in the circumoesophageal nerve ring of cone snails (Figure 1C) (Safavi-Hemami et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence data shown in Figure 1C and citation to Safavi-Hemami et al., 2016.

claim: Venom insulin sequences exhibit pronounced sequence divergence with very few conserved amino acids.
source: Overall, venom insulin sequences exhibit pronounced sequence divergence with very few conserved amino acids.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The relatively well conserved amino acids in venom insulins include the first four residues in the A chain, Gly8, Ser9 and Leu18 in the B chain and all six cysteines.
source: The few relatively well conserved amino acids include the first four residues in the A chain, Gly8, Ser9 and Leu18 in the B chain and all six cysteines (see Sequence Logo in Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TyrB15 previously identified to serve as a surrogate in Con-Ins G1 for the missing B chain C-terminus of human insulin is only moderately conserved.
source: Strikingly, the two residues (TyrB15 and TyrB20) previously identified to serve as surrogates in Con-Ins G1 for the missing B chain C-terminus of human insulin are only moderately conserved (TyrB15) or hypervariable (TyrB20).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TyrB20 previously identified to serve as a surrogate in Con-Ins G1 for the missing B chain C-terminus of human insulin is hypervariable.
source: Strikingly, the two residues (TyrB15 and TyrB20) previously identified to serve as surrogates in Con-Ins G1 for the missing B chain C-terminus of human insulin are only moderately conserved (TyrB15) or hypervariable (TyrB20).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: All novel insulin sequences were successfully synthesized using Fmoc peptide chemistry.
source: Here, all novel insulin sequences were successfully synthesized using Fmoc peptide chemistry.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental methods described in the manuscript.

claim: There is no difference in activity between Con-Ins G1 containing a diselenide bond and native Con-Ins G1.
source: We previously reported that there is no difference in activity between Con-Ins G1 containing a diselenide bond and native Con-Ins G1 (11) and similar observations have been made for other peptides (Walewska et al., 2009; Muttenthaler et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Behavioral observations of C. geographus and C. tulipa have demonstrated that these species prey on fish and release compounds into the water prior to prey capture.
source: Indeed, behavioral observations of C. geographus and C. tulipa have demonstrated that these species prey on fish and release compounds into the water prior to prey capture (Olivera et al., 2015) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Olivera et al., 2015.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis places C. kinoshitai within fish-hunters.
source: While no behavioral data is available for C. kinoshitai, phylogenetic analysis places this species within fish-hunters (the majority of cone snail species prey on marine worms and some prey on snails) (Olivera et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Olivera et al., 2015.

claim: Following STZ treatment, blood glucose levels were significantly elevated from 65.9 ± 4.8 mg/dL (n = 11) to 393.3 ± 10.2 mg/dL (n = 7).
source: Following STZ treatment, blood glucose levels were significantly elevated from 65.9 ± 4.8 mg/dL (n = 11) to 393.3 ± 10.2 mg/dL (n = 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the zebrafish STZ assay.

claim: Administration of venom insulins at 65 ng peptide/g body weight significantly lowered blood glucose levels for all venom insulins tested.
source: Administration of venom insulins at 65 ng peptide/g body weight significantly lowered blood glucose levels for all venom insulins tested (Figure 2) with values ranging from 77.8 ± 39.8 mg/dL for Con-Ins T1A (p<0.0001, n = 5) to 199.2 ± 39.8 mg/dL for Con-Ins T2 (p<0.0067, n = 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Con-Ins T1A lowered blood glucose to 77.8 ± 39.8 mg/dL (p<0.0001, n = 5).
source: Administration of venom insulins at 65 ng peptide/g body weight significantly lowered blood glucose levels for all venom insulins tested (Figure 2) with values ranging from 77.8 ± 39.8 mg/dL for Con-Ins T1A (p<0.0001, n = 5) to 199.2 ± 39.8 mg/dL for Con-Ins T2 (p<0.0067, n = 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Con-Ins T2 lowered blood glucose to 199.2 ± 39.8 mg/dL (p<0.0067, n = 5).
source: Administration of venom insulins at 65 ng peptide/g body weight significantly lowered blood glucose levels for all venom insulins tested (Figure 2) with values ranging from 77.8 ± 39.8 mg/dL for Con-Ins T1A (p<0.0001, n = 5) to 199.2 ± 39.8 mg/dL for Con-Ins T2 (p<0.0067, n = 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: 65 ng of human insulin/g body weight reduces blood glucose to 92.0 ± 17.4 mg/dL.
source: For comparison, 65 ng of human insulin (hIns)/g body weight reduces blood glucose to 92.0 ± 17.4 mg/dL (Safavi-Hemami et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Safavi-Hemami et al., 2015.

claim: Venom insulins are capable of binding to and activating the fish insulin receptor.
source: This demonstrates that venom insulins are capable of binding to and activating the fish insulin receptor, supporting their biological role in inducing insulin shock in fish prey.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the zebrafish STZ assay data shown in Figure 2.

claim: All seven venom insulins bound to the hIR with affinities ranging from IC50 9.92 nM for Con-Ins T1A to IC50 275.2 nM for Con-Ins K2.
source: All seven venom insulins bound to the hIR with affinities ranging from IC50 9.92 nM (7.75–12.68 nM; 95% CI) for the most potent insulin Con-Ins T1A to IC50 275.2 nM (162.2–487.6 nM; 95 % CI) for Con-Ins K2 (n = 2 biological replicates with three technical replicates each; the IC50 indicates half-maximal inhibitory concentration; Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The affinity of human insulin for hIR-B is IC50 0.44 nM (0.40–0.49 nM; 95 % CI).
source: For comparison, the affinity of hIns is ~20 fold higher than the most potent venom insulin Con-Ins T1A [hIns IC50 0.44 nM (0.40–0.49 nM; 95 % CI)].
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Con-Ins G1 potently activates the human insulin receptor with an EC50 of 16.28 nM (95% CI: 7.3–36.4 nM).
source: As previously shown, Con-Ins G1 potently activates the human insulins receptor, albeit at lower potency when compared to human insulin (EC50 of Con-Ins G1 16.28 nM; 95% CI: 7.3–36.4 nM; EC50 of human insulin 1.5 nM; 95% CI: 1.1–2.1 nM, in which the EC50 indicates half-maximal effective concentration) (Figure 4A and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and E.

claim: Human insulin activates the human insulin receptor with an EC50 of 1.5 nM (95% CI: 1.1–2.1 nM).
source: As previously shown, Con-Ins G1 potently activates the human insulins receptor, albeit at lower potency when compared to human insulin (EC50 of Con-Ins G1 16.28 nM; 95% CI: 7.3–36.4 nM; EC50 of human insulin 1.5 nM; 95% CI: 1.1–2.1 nM, in which the EC50 indicates half-maximal effective concentration) (Figure 4A and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and E.

claim: Con-Ins G3 was significantly less potent at the hIR-B with an EC50 of 242.0 nM (95% CI: 101.3–578.5 nM).
source: The other insulin identified from C. geographus, Con-Ins G3, was significantly less potent at the hIR-B with an EC50 of 242.0 nM, 95% CI: 101.3–578.5 nM).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and E.

claim: All three insulins identified from C. tulipa were potently active at the hIR-B with activities comparable to Con-Ins G1.
source: In contrast, all three insulins identified from C. tulipa were potently active at the hIR-B with activities comparable to Con-Ins G1 (EC50 of Con-Ins T1A 12.0, 95% CI: 9.7–15.0 nM; EC50 of Con-Ins T1B 12.0 nM, 95% CI: 10.2–13.8 nM; EC50 of Con-Ins T2 15.5 nM, 95% CI: 11.9–20.2 nM) (n = 4 technical replicates; Figure 4B and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and E.

claim: Con-Ins T1A activates hIR-B with an EC50 of 12.0 nM (95% CI: 9.7–15.0 nM).
source: In contrast, all three insulins identified from C. tulipa were potently active at the hIR-B with activities comparable to Con-Ins G1 (EC50 of Con-Ins T1A 12.0, 95% CI: 9.7–15.0 nM; EC50 of Con-Ins T1B 12.0 nM, 95% CI: 10.2–13.8 nM; EC50 of Con-Ins T2 15.5 nM, 95% CI: 11.9–20.2 nM) (n = 4 technical replicates; Figure 4B and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and E.

claim: Con-Ins T1B activates hIR-B with an EC50 of 12.0 nM (95% CI: 10.2–13.8 nM).
source: In contrast, all three insulins identified from C. tulipa were potently active at the hIR-B with activities comparable to Con-Ins G1 (EC50 of Con-Ins T1A 12.0, 95% CI: 9.7–15.0 nM; EC50 of Con-Ins T1B 12.0 nM, 95% CI: 10.2–13.8 nM; EC50 of Con-Ins T2 15.5 nM, 95% CI: 11.9–20.2 nM) (n = 4 technical replicates; Figure 4B and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and E.

claim: Con-Ins T2 activates hIR-B with an EC50 of 15.5 nM (95% CI: 11.9–20.2 nM).
source: In contrast, all three insulins identified from C. tulipa were potently active at the hIR-B with activities comparable to Con-Ins G1 (EC50 of Con-Ins T1A 12.0, 95% CI: 9.7–15.0 nM; EC50 of Con-Ins T1B 12.0 nM, 95% CI: 10.2–13.8 nM; EC50 of Con-Ins T2 15.5 nM, 95% CI: 11.9–20.2 nM) (n = 4 technical replicates; Figure 4B and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and E.

claim: Con-Ins K1 activates hIR-B with an EC50 of 30.45 nM (95 % CI 16.9–55.0 nM).
source: C. kinoshitai insulins showed variable activity with an EC50 of 30.45 nM (95 % CI 16.9–55.0 nM) for Con-Ins K1 and 373.2 nM (95 % CI 61.6–2262.0 nM) for Con-Ins K2 (Figure 4C and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and E.

claim: Con-Ins K2 activates hIR-B with an EC50 of 373.2 nM (95 % CI 61.6–2262.0 nM).
source: C. kinoshitai insulins showed variable activity with an EC50 of 30.45 nM (95 % CI 16.9–55.0 nM) for Con-Ins K1 and 373.2 nM (95 % CI 61.6–2262.0 nM) for Con-Ins K2 (Figure 4C and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and E.

claim: The ability of venom insulins to bind to the hIR correlates with downstream signaling activity.
source: Overall, the ability of venom insulins to bind to the hIR correlates with downstream signaling activity although some differences can be observed.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Con-Ins T2 and Con-Ins K1 have higher activation potency than would be expected from their receptor binding potencies.

claim: Insulin and related peptides form a large superfamily of peptide hormones that is found throughout the animal kingdom.

claim: In vertebrates, insulin is synthesized in pancreatic β-cells and is the key regulator of carbohydrate and fat metabolism.
source: In vertebrates, insulin is synthesized in pancreatic β-cells and is the key regulator of carbohydrate and fat metabolism (Blumenthal, 2010).

claim: The discovery of an insulin in C. geographus that is unprecedentedly small and shares the disulfide framework with vertebrate insulin indicated that this insulin had evolved to rapidly and effectively induce insulin shock in fish prey.

claim: The large majority of the ~800 extant cone snail species prey on worms.
source: The large majority of the ~800 extant cone snail species prey on worms.

claim: Fish- and snail-hunting behaviors are believed to have only evolved in very few clades within the cone snail genus.
source: Fish- and snail-hunting behaviors are believed to have only evolved in very few clades within this large genus.

claim: Within fish-hunters, only a small subset of species expresses insulins that mimic fish insulins (C. geographus and C. tulipa from the Gastridium clade).

claim: Cone snail venom peptides are known for their rapid rate of gene duplications and sequence diversification with nearly no overlap in each toxin repertoire, even between sister species.
source: Cone snail venom peptides are known for their rapid rate of gene duplications and sequence diversification with nearly no overlap in each toxin repertoire, even between sister species (Li et al., 2017).

claim: The drastic sequence divergences of venom insulins is consistent with the rapid evolution of cone snail toxins.
source: The drastic sequence divergences of venom insulins reported here is consistent with the rapid evolution of cone snail toxins.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing venom insulin sequences to known patterns of cone snail toxin evolution.

claim: All venom insulins potently lower blood glucose in a zebrafish model of diabetes suggesting that diverse strategies have evolved to bind to and activate the fish insulin receptor.
source: Yet, all potently lower blood glucose in a zebrafish model of diabetes suggesting that, in cone snails, diverse strategies have evolved to bind to and activate the fish insulin receptor.

claim: Five of the seven venom insulins tested show higher activity at the hIR-B than the B-chain truncated human insulin analog DOI.

claim: Mutation of HisB10 to Asp in human insulin leads to a dramatic increase in hIR activation.
